doc.title: Mat Domber interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Bob Haggart and the first March of Jazz party
summary: Haggart plays a St. Petersburg concert, becomes a friend, and his 80th birthday leads to the first March of Jazz.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: concert in St. Petersburg and for some reason or other the bass player who was supposed to be playing, this was about 1991 I would say, the bass player who was supposed to be playing with us couldn’t show up. So we were nervous about a bass player and somebody said to Rick there’s a guy by the name of Bob Haggart, who is a well known bass player, who lives in Venice, Florida. Why don’t you give him a call and see if he’d be interested. I thought to myself I knew about the Bob Crosby Band, I knew about the World’s Greatest Jazz Band and all of that. I said Bob Haggart? He wouldn’t want to come up here to St. Petersburg to play with us. But I called him. And Bob said, “Great, I’d love it.” Bob was the kind of guy, a fantastic musician of course. But also he was a man without really any ego in the sense that he just loved to play. He wouldn’t care if he was playing with a good group at a local bar, he would love it. If he was playing at Carnegie Hall he would love it as long as the musical atmosphere was one that he enjoyed being with. So he came up, he didn’t care about the money or anything else. And he played. And from that point on we became friends. And he was on a couple of records with us. And then one day we were doing a record, I’ll never forget, in Orlando with Chuck Hedges, a wonderful clarinet player. Bob was playing bass. And we stayed together at a hotel for the record session. And this was like 1993. And we were having breakfast with Bob and his wife Wendy. And I happened to make a casual remark, you know, that it’d be lovely to put on a jazz party or a jazz festival because that’s a good way to market the music and it’s a good way to expose the music. And Wendy said, “Well you know next year in 1994 my husband’s going to be 80 years old.” And I said, “By God that’s a wonderful way to present a jazz party in honor of Bob Haggart’s 80th birthday.” And that was our first March of Jazz. And that, you see, led me into a whole different range of music. It led me into the people who played with Bob and the people who Bob knew, because in order to put on the party I said Bob, “It’s your birthday, you pick the musicians.” So who did he pick? Flip Phillips, Bob Wilber, Kenny Davern, Ralph Sutton, the people who were meaningful. Bobby Rosengarden. I mean the people who were meaningful to him in his career, who were still alive. Yank Lawson, and were playing, and that got me started with a whole new group of people. So everything happened sort of by chance. It was never designed. At that party I was talking to Flip Phillips and his wife Miki said, “Well you know next year Flip is gong to be 80 years old.” So that was our second March of Jazz party and then it just went on until 2004. We put on ten of them and then it was enough.
